Two hundred rows, ten thousand columns of random numbers, and a label that's a coin flip. Cross-validated, this model scores eighty-five percent. Nothing in it can predict anything. Question six finds where the eighty-five came from. Language models didn't retire classical machine learning, and the first thing an ML round still tests is whether a model works on data it hasn't seen. Twelve questions. Ten are worked through: why models fail on new data, how to measure that honestly, and which number to report. Two are quick.

Question one. Explain the bias-variance trade-off, and its decomposition. Bias is error from a model too simple for the pattern; variance, from fitting one training sample's quirks. With noise no model can remove, bias squared, variance and noise sum to the expected squared error on new data. A simulation can measure all three. Draw five hundred training sets of fifty points from a known curve, and fit a tree to each. At one point on the curve, the stumps' predictions bunch together, off target: that's bias. Trees six deep centre on the target, and scatter: that's variance. Averaged along the curve, a stump's error is point two oh: point oh seven bias, point oh four variance, point oh nine noise. Depth three is lowest, at point one four, and deeper trees climb back up, almost all of it variance. The follow-up is what fixes each. Give the depth-six tree ten times the data, and its variance falls from point oh eight to point oh three. The stump's bias doesn't fall at all. On a real problem there's one dataset and no known curve, so you read the two from training and validation error.
